indicator_definition:
The indicator is part of the EU Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) indicator set. It is used to monitor progress towards SDG 1 on ending poverty in all its forms everywhere and SDG 10 on reducing inequality within and among countries which are embedded in the European Commission’s Priority under 'Supporting people, strenghtening our societes and our social model'. This indicator corresponds to the sum of people who are: at risk of poverty after social transfers, severely materially and socially deprived, or living in households with very low work intensity. Individuals are counted only once, even if they are affected by more than one of these occurrences.
•	People are considered at risk of poverty after social transfers if their equivalent disposable income is not higher than the poverty risk threshold, which is set at 60% of the national median equivalent disposable income.
•	Severe material and social deprivation rate is the share of the population experiencing a forced lack of at least 7 out of 13 deprivation items (6 relate to the individual, and 7 to the household)
rationale: Poverty and social exclusion are harmful to individual lives and limit people's opportunities to reach their full potential by affecting their health and well-being and reducing educational outcomes. This, in turn, reduces opportunities for a successful life and further increases the risk of poverty. Without an effective system of education, healthcare, social protection, tax relief, and employment, the risk of poverty is passed from one generation to the next. This causes the persistence of poverty and thereby creates even more inequality, which can lead to long-term loss of economic productivity of entire groups of society and hinder inclusive and sustainable economic growth.
methodology_characteristics: The data used for this indicator is based on the Europe-wide harmonised annual survey on income and living conditions (EU-SILC). In the 2020 survey year, EU-SILC underwent extensive methodological revisions and was integrated into the microcensus in response to increasing demands for up-to-date data and the provision of more detailed regional results. As a result of this realignment, the data from 2020 onwards is not comparable with that of previous years. Since 2021, Regulation (EU) 2019/1700 provides for requirements relating to geographical coverage, detailed sample characteristics, including sub-sampling, in accordance with Annex III, common data collection periods, common standards for editing and imputation, weighting, estimation and variance estimation.
